title: Green synthesis and characterization of CuO PANI nanocomposite for efficient Pb (II) adsorption from contaminated water

predicted_errors.error_location: All embedded main figures (the images inserted as Figures 0–7, including the purported XRD, FTIR, SEM/EDS, XPS, adsorption, and model plots)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The supplied figure files do not display the scientific plots, spectra, micrographs, elemental maps, axes, legends, or fitted curves described in the manuscript. Instead, they contain extensive unrelated repeated text/artwork (for example repeated strings such as “CEIQ,” “AhCEIA,” and unrelated prose-like content). Thus the stated peak positions, BET changes, EDS compositions, adsorption trends, and fitting claims cannot be checked against the figures. The figures must be replaced with the actual, legible experimental figures and captions.

The manuscript states that, in the composite, “some peaks in pristine g-CuO NPs disappear,” but immediately states, “Despite this interaction, all the characteristic CuO peaks were still visible.” Both statements cannot be true as written. The authors must specify which CuO reflections remain detectable and which are absent or obscured.

predicted_errors.error_location: XRD discussion of g-CuO peak indexing, Fig. 1b
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The reported CuO reflection assignments are materially wrong/internally confused. For tenorite CuO (JCPDS 48-1548), the usual sequence includes approximately 32.5° (110), 35.5° (-111), 38.7° (111), 48.7° (-202), 53.5° (020), 58.3° (202), 61.5° (-113), 66.2° (-311), and 68.1° (220). The manuscript instead assigns 49° to (202), 61° to (022), and 68° to (-202), while assigning both 49° and 58° to (202). These are not the listed JCPDS assignments and require correction.

The described synthesis mixes 0.01 M CuSO4 with aqueous plant extract, heats it, centrifuges, washes, and dries it, but includes no alkaline precipitating agent, pH adjustment, calcination, or other stated oxidation/decomposition step that would convert soluble Cu(II) sulfate into stoichiometric CuO. The procedure as written does not chemically establish formation of CuO rather than adsorbed Cu salts, copper complexes, Cu2O/Cu species, or a poorly specified plant-derived precipitate. The claimed CuO identity therefore cannot be supported by the stated synthesis protocol without missing steps or additional chemical evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Batch adsorption methods versus pH-effect experiment
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The batch protocol says that 25 mg of CuO/PANI was placed in 100 mL Pb solution, corresponding to an adsorbent concentration of 250 mg/L. The pH experiment instead states that it used “a CuO/PANI dosage of 25 mg/L.” These differ by a factor of ten. The actual mass used in the pH experiment, and hence all dosage-dependent capacities and removal values, is ambiguous.

The reported maximum removal occurs at pH 6, close to the range where Pb(II) hydrolysis/lead hydroxide precipitation can materially reduce dissolved Pb. The paper provides no Pb-only pH-control blank, no speciation calculation, and no explicit filtration/separation protocol distinguishing precipitated Pb from adsorbed Pb. Consequently, the reported 95.25% ‘adsorption’ at pH 6 cannot be attributed to adsorption on CuO/PANI.

The text states: “When the pH rises above 6, lead ions precipitate as hydroxides, and removal efficiency decreases.” If the measured endpoint is dissolved Pb concentration, Pb hydroxide precipitation would itself lower dissolved Pb and generally increase apparent removal unless the precipitate is explicitly redissolved, excluded, or the analytical workflow is otherwise changed. The asserted direction of the effect is chemically/logically unsupported and conflicts with the stated removal equation.

The manuscript says the XPS survey spectrum showed “Cu1s.” This is an incorrect designation for the Cu feature discussed later at 934.80 and 954.44 eV: those are Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2 peaks. Cu 1s has a binding energy near 9 keV and would not be the ordinary survey feature at these energies. The survey assignment must be corrected.

predicted_errors.error_location: XPS after Pb adsorption, Pb oxidation-state interpretation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The study begins with Pb(NO3)2 and supplies no oxidant or electrochemical process capable of converting adsorbed Pb(II) to Pb(IV), yet it claims that the post-adsorption XPS contains Pb4+ as well as Pb(II). Moreover, the two stated Pb4+ energies, 141.08 and 138.43 eV, differ by only 2.65 eV, not the approximately 4.8–4.9 eV Pb 4f spin-orbit separation. This is not a physically valid Pb 4f doublet assignment. The Pb oxidation-state fitting and any mechanistic conclusion based on Pb(IV) must be reanalysed.

The O 1s component at 531.67 eV is assigned to “O=N.” Neither polyaniline nor CuO contains an N=O group, and no nitrogen-oxygen reagent or oxidation step is reported. This assignment is chemically unsupported; an O 1s component cannot be assigned to O=N in this material without independent evidence of nitroso/nitro species.

The CuO Raman assignments are inconsistent with established monoclinic tenorite modes. The manuscript assigns 421 cm−1 to Ag and 538 and 787 cm−1 to B1g and B2g. The commonly reported CuO Raman modes are near 298 cm−1 (Ag), 346 cm−1 (B1g), and 632 cm−1 (B2g), with modest nanoparticle shifts not normally sufficient to validate the stated 421/538/787 cm−1 assignments. The reported assignments need evidence or correction before they can be used to confirm CuO.

The paragraph says that morphology after Pb adsorption is “depicted in Fig. 4(c),” but then states that Pb appears in the EDS spectrum “as shown in Fig. 3(c).” Given that the preceding panels are described as Fig. 3(a) and Fig. 3(b), the post-adsorption panel is inconsistently cited as both Fig. 4(c) and Fig. 3(c). This prevents unambiguous identification of the claimed SEM/EDS evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and adsorption-methods/results claims of “outstanding adsorption capacity”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The methods define only percentage removal, % removal = ((C0 − Ct)/C0) × 100, and do not provide the adsorption-capacity equation q = (C0 − Ce)V/m, equilibrium-contact-time protocol, Pb analytical method, calibration, replicates, or uncertainty. Yet the abstract asserts “outstanding adsorption capacity” and claims isotherm/kinetic model superiority. Without a defined and reported q_e dataset, analytical method, error estimates, and actual fitted parameter values, the capacity and model-based performance claim is not supported by the described methodology.
